text: Earth's diameter is about 12,740 km
as_written: about twelve thousand seven hundred and forty kilometres across
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (mean radius 6,371 km)

text: The Kola Superdeep Borehole is in northwest Russia near the Norwegian border
as_written: in northwest Russia, near the border with Norway
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project records, Kola Peninsula, Murmansk Oblast

text: Drilling began in 1970
as_written: Soviet engineers began drilling in nineteen seventy
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project records (Kozlovsky, Scientific American 1984)

text: Kola reached 12,262 m in 1989, the deepest borehole ever drilled
as_written: twelve thousand two hundred and sixty-two metres
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project records; Guinness World Records

text: Challenger Deep is nearly 11 km deep
as_written: which is nearly eleven kilometres down
source: NOAA Ocean Exploration; UNH Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping 2010 survey (about 10,984 m)

text: Mount Everest is just under 9 km tall
as_written: at just under nine kilometres
source: 2020 joint China-Nepal survey (8,848.86 m)

text: The Kola hole is about 23 cm wide
as_written: about twenty-three centimetres wide
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project records (commonly cited 23 cm / 9 in diameter)

text: 12.262 km is under 0.1 percent of Earth's 12,742 km diameter
as_written: less than one tenth of one percent of the way through the planet
source: Arithmetic from Kola depth and NASA Earth Fact Sheet diameter (0.096 percent)

text: At Kola's pace of about 12.3 km in about 19 years, the full diameter would take roughly 20,000 years
as_written: roughly twenty thousand years
source: Arithmetic from Kola depth (12,262 m, 1970 to 1989) and Earth diameter (about 1,040 times deeper)

text: Expected bottom temperature was about 100 C
as_written: around one hundred degrees Celsius at the bottom
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project reports (Kozlovsky, Scientific American 1984)

text: Measured bottom temperature was about 180 C
as_written: about one hundred and eighty
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project reports (Kozlovsky, Scientific American 1984)

text: Rock at depth behaved plastically and walls tried to close in
as_written: did not behave like a rigid slab, and the walls kept trying to close in on the drill
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project reports (Kozlovsky, Scientific American 1984)

text: Drilling ended in 1992
as_written: Drilling ended in nineteen ninety-two
source: Kola Superdeep Borehole project records

text: A free-falling body drops about 4.9 m in the first second
as_written: you fall about five metres
source: Newtonian kinematics with standard gravity 9.80665 m/s squared (NIST)

text: After one second of free fall speed is about 9.8 m/s
as_written: nearly ten metres per second
source: Newtonian kinematics with standard gravity (NIST)

text: After 10 s of vacuum free fall speed is about 98 m/s and drop about 490 m
as_written: close to a hundred metres per second, and you would have dropped nearly five hundred metres
source: Newtonian kinematics with standard gravity (NIST)

text: Speed of sound in air is about 340 m/s, reached after about 35 s at 9.8 m/s squared
as_written: Around thirty-five seconds in, you would pass the speed of sound in air, about three hundred and forty metres per second
source: International Standard Atmosphere (340.3 m/s at 15 C); kinematics

text: Belly-down skydiver terminal velocity is about 55 m/s, about 200 km/h
as_written: roughly fifty-five metres per second, which is about two hundred kilometres an hour
source: United States Parachute Association (about 120 mph); NASA Glenn terminal velocity page

text: Terminal velocity falls as air density rises, and air density rises with depth
as_written: So the deeper you go, the slower the fastest possible fall becomes
source: Drag equation (NASA Glenn); hydrostatic atmosphere

text: Earth rotates once in about 24 hours
as_written: The planet turns once every twenty-four hours, near enough
source: International Earth Rotation and Reference Systems Service

text: Equatorial surface rotation speed is about 465 m/s
as_written: about four hundred and sixty-five metres per second
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet; IERS

text: That is about 1,670 km/h
as_written: roughly sixteen hundred and seventy kilometres an hour
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet; IERS

text: Coriolis eastward drift of a freely falling body, x = (1/3) omega g t cubed, reaches about 1 m in roughly 16 s, so a 2 m hole is hit in under half a minute
as_written: you would be scraping the wall in well under half a minute
source: Classical mechanics, Coriolis deflection of falling bodies (Goldstein, Classical Mechanics)

text: The effect vanishes on the rotation axis
as_written: At the poles, right on the axis, it vanishes
source: Classical mechanics, Coriolis deflection scales with cosine of latitude

text: The North Pole is on drifting sea ice over several km of Arctic Ocean
as_written: The North Pole sits on drifting sea ice above several kilometres of ocean
source: NOAA; International Bathymetric Chart of the Arctic Ocean

text: About 35 km is fallen in about 85 s at constant gravity
as_written: At about eighty-five seconds, you have dropped thirty-five kilometres
source: Newtonian kinematics with standard gravity

text: Continental crust is about 30 to 50 km thick, oceanic crust 5 to 10 km
as_written: Continental crust runs from about thirty to fifty kilometres thick, and under the oceans it is only five to ten
source: USGS

text: The Moho was identified by Mohorovicic in 1909 from seismic wave behaviour
as_written: Andrija Mohorovičić, the Croatian seismologist who found it in nineteen oh nine
source: Standard seismology history (Mohorovicic 1909)

text: After about 85 s speed is about 830 m/s
as_written: more than eight hundred metres per second
source: Newtonian kinematics with standard gravity

text: Mponeng gold mine reaches nearly 4 km
as_written: reaches nearly four kilometres down
source: AngloGold Ashanti (Mponeng, about 3.9 to 4 km)

text: Rock at Mponeng exceeds 60 C
as_written: more than sixty degrees Celsius
source: AngloGold Ashanti; mining engineering literature on virgin rock temperature at Mponeng

text: The mine is cooled with ice-making plants
as_written: air cooled by plants that make ice
source: AngloGold Ashanti; mining ventilation and cooling literature

text: Rock begins to glow dull red near 525 C (Draper point)
as_written: about five hundred and twenty-five degrees Celsius
source: Draper point, J. W. Draper 1847; standard physics references

text: The mantle is nearly 3,000 km thick (about 2,890 km)
as_written: nearly three thousand kilometres of it
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981); USGS

text: The mantle is solid rock, not magma, flowing over millions of years
as_written: It is not an ocean of magma. It is solid rock
source: USGS

text: Tectonic plates move a few centimetres per year
as_written: which is a few centimetres a year
source: USGS

text: Lithostatic pressure rises about 27 MPa per km, about 270 atmospheres
as_written: roughly twenty-seven million pascals of pressure, which is about two hundred and seventy times the pressure of the air around you
source: Lithostatic pressure P = density x g x depth, with crustal density about 2.7 g/cm3 (Turcotte and Schubert, Geodynamics)

text: Diamond anvil cell samples are often narrower than a human hair
as_written: the samples are often narrower than a human hair
source: High-pressure mineral physics literature on diamond anvil cells (Mao and Bell)

text: In a uniform-density Earth, gravity falls linearly with depth, so half-way you weigh half
as_written: Halfway to the centre you weigh half as much
source: Newton's shell theorem

text: Earth's mean density is about 5.5 times water
as_written: about five and a half times that of water
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (5,514 kg/m3)

text: Inner core density is about 13 g/cm3
as_written: about thirteen times denser than water
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981)

text: Gravity stays near 9.8 m/s squared through the mantle
as_written: nine point eight metres per second squared through the mantle
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981)

text: Gravity peaks near 10.7 m/s squared at the core-mantle boundary
as_written: about ten point seven
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981)

text: Below that, gravity falls roughly linearly to zero at the centre
as_written: roughly in a straight line, until it reaches zero at the centre
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model (Dziewonski and Anderson 1981)

text: Core-mantle boundary is at about 2,890 km depth
as_written: about two thousand eight hundred and ninety kilometres
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model; USGS

text: Outer core is about 2,260 km thick (2,890 to 5,150 km)
as_written: about two thousand two hundred and sixty kilometres thick
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model

text: Shear waves cannot pass through liquid, revealing the liquid outer core
as_written: One kind of wave, the shear wave, cannot travel through liquid
source: Standard seismology (Oldham 1906; Gutenberg 1914); USGS

text: Flowing outer core generates Earth's magnetic field
as_written: flowing metal generates the magnetic field that steers your compass
source: NASA; USGS (geodynamo)

text: Inner core boundary is at about 5,150 km depth
as_written: about five thousand one hundred and fifty kilometres down
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model

text: Inge Lehmann identified the solid inner core in 1936
as_written: In nineteen thirty-six, the Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann
source: Lehmann 1936, 'P prime', Bureau Central Seismologique International

text: Inner core radius is about 1,220 km, about 70 percent of the Moon's radius
as_written: about twelve hundred and twenty kilometres, around seventy percent of the radius of the Moon
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model (1,221 km); NASA Moon Fact Sheet (1,737.4 km)

text: Pressure at Earth's centre is about 360 GPa, about 3.5 million atmospheres
as_written: roughly three and a half million times the pressure of the air at the surface
source: Preliminary Reference Earth Model (about 364 GPa)

text: Sun's surface temperature is about 5,800 K
as_written: about five thousand eight hundred kelvin
source: IAU 2015 nominal solar effective temperature 5,772 K; NASA Sun Fact Sheet

text: Inner core boundary temperature estimates range about 5,000 to 6,000 K and are contested
as_written: between about five thousand and six thousand kelvin
source: Anzellini et al., Science 2013 (about 6,230 K); Alfe et al. and earlier estimates near 5,400 K

text: Uniform-Earth fall speed at the centre is sqrt(gR), about 7.9 km/s, about 28,000 km/h
as_written: about seven point nine kilometres per second, or about twenty-eight thousand kilometres an hour
source: Newtonian mechanics, sqrt(g R) with R = 6,371 km (NASA Earth Fact Sheet)

text: With a dense core the central speed is higher than in the uniform model
as_written: In the real Earth, with its dense core, it is higher
source: Klotz 2015, Am. J. Phys. 83, 231; Preliminary Reference Earth Model

text: Realistic-density fall time through the centre is about 38 minutes
as_written: Thirty-eight minutes after you stepped off
source: Klotz, 'The gravity tunnel in a non-uniform Earth', American Journal of Physics 83, 231 (2015)

text: Klotz published in 2015 in the American Journal of Physics
as_written: who in twenty fifteen worked out the fall time
source: Klotz, American Journal of Physics 83, 231 (2015)

text: Uniform-density fall time is about 42 minutes
as_written: you get about forty-two minutes instead
source: Simple harmonic motion, half of 2 pi sqrt(R/g); Cooper, Am. J. Phys. 1966

text: In a uniform Earth every straight frictionless tunnel takes the same time
as_written: the trip takes the same forty-two minutes
source: Cooper, 'Travel time through the Earth', American Journal of Physics 34 (1966)

text: A surface-skimming orbit takes about 84 minutes
as_written: which is about eighty-four minutes
source: Orbital mechanics, 2 pi sqrt(R/g) with Earth radius 6,371 km

text: About 71 percent of Earth's surface is ocean
as_written: About seventy-one percent of the planet's surface is ocean
source: NOAA; USGS

text: Parts of Spain are antipodal to parts of New Zealand
as_written: Parts of Spain sit directly opposite parts of New Zealand
source: Antipode calculation from geographic coordinates (for example Wellington 41.3 S 174.8 E against 41.3 N 5.2 W in Spain)

text: Typical continental geothermal gradient is 25 to 30 C per km
as_written: twenty-five to thirty degrees Celsius for every kilometre
source: USGS; standard geophysics texts (Turcotte and Schubert, Geodynamics)

text: A 2 m diameter hole through 12,742 km has volume about 40 million cubic metres
as_written: about forty million cubic metres
source: Cylinder volume pi r squared L with r = 1 m, L = 12,742 km

text: An Olympic pool holds about 2,500 cubic metres, so 40 million is about 16,000 pools
as_written: about sixteen thousand Olympic swimming pools
source: World Aquatics minimum 50 m x 25 m x 2 m pool (2,500 m3); arithmetic

text: Earth's volume is about 1.08 trillion cubic km
as_written: roughly one point oh eight trillion cubic kilometres
source: NASA Goddard Earth Fact Sheet (1.08321 x 10^12 km3)

text: Oceans hold about 1.3 billion cubic km of water
as_written: about one point three billion cubic kilometres of water
source: NOAA National Geophysical Data Center (about 1.335 billion km3)

text: Gravitational time dilation: clocks run slower deeper in a gravitational field
as_written: time runs slower the deeper you sit in a gravitational field
source: Einstein's general theory of relativity; Pound and Rebka 1960

text: GPS clocks run about 45 microseconds per day fast from weaker gravity
as_written: about forty-five millionths of a second per day
source: Ashby, 'Relativity in the Global Positioning System', Living Reviews in Relativity 2003

text: GPS clocks run about 7 microseconds per day slow from speed
as_written: about seven millionths of a second per day because of their speed
source: Ashby, Living Reviews in Relativity 2003

text: Net GPS offset is about 38 microseconds per day
as_written: roughly thirty-eight millionths of a second a day
source: Ashby, Living Reviews in Relativity 2003

text: JILA measured gravitational redshift across about a millimetre in 2022
as_written: In twenty twenty-two, physicists at the JILA institute in Colorado measured the effect across a height of about a millimetre
source: Bothwell et al., 'Resolving the gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale atomic sample', Nature 602, 420 (2022)

text: Feynman remarked the centre should be a day or two younger
as_written: a day or two younger than the surface
source: Feynman Lectures on Gravitation, as cited by Uggerhoj, Mikkelsen and Faye (2016)

text: Uggerhoj, Mikkelsen and Faye published 'The young centre of the Earth' in 2016
as_written: In twenty sixteen, three Danish physicists, Ulrik Uggerhøj, Robert Mikkelsen and Jan Faye
source: Uggerhoj, Mikkelsen and Faye, European Journal of Physics 37, 035602 (2016)

text: Earth's age is about 4.5 billion years
as_written: about four and a half billion years
source: USGS (about 4.54 billion years)

text: The core is about 2.5 years younger than the crust
as_written: about two and a half years less than the crust
source: Uggerhoj, Mikkelsen and Faye, European Journal of Physics 37, 035602 (2016)
